practice.prompt: Prove that when you add two multiples of 4, you always get a multiple of 4.
practice.slot: No drawing needed; live text only.
practice.solution: By the definition of a multiple, m=4r and n=4s for integers r, s. Then m+n=4r+4s=4(r+s). Since integers are closed under addition, r+s is an integer, so m+n is a multiple of 4.
practice.check: Difference is a parallel independent result: m-n=4(r-s). The sum proof uses only a definition, distributivity and integer closure, not selected numerical cases.
practice.diagram: No geometric diagram is needed; use live mathematical text.

practice.prompt: Use an indirect proof to show: if the square of an integer is odd, then the integer is odd. Then say which integers have a square of 81.
practice.slot: No drawing needed; live text only.
practice.solution: Assume n² is odd but n is not odd. Every integer is even or odd, so n=2k for an integer k. Then n²=4k²=2(2k²) is even, contradicting the given odd square. Therefore n is odd. For the specified square the possible integers are plus or minus 9, both odd.
practice.check: The contrapositive supplies a second route: an even integer 2k has even square 4k². This is equivalent to the claim. No ruler postulate, triangle theorem or drawing is used.
practice.diagram: No geometric diagram is needed; use live mathematical text.

practice.prompt: Two segments in a drawing have no marks, but they seem equal in length. Were you given that they are equal? How could you make sure?
practice.slot: Two unmarked segments. Answer side only: a ruler panel with marks at 0 and 5, and at 7 and 12.
practice.solution: No. Appearance supplies neither measurement nor a hypothesis. If endpoints are on an explicitly calibrated ruler at 0, 5 and 7, 12, both distances equal 5; otherwise obtain an equality mark, measurement assumption or proof.
practice.check: An example that fits every given but breaks the claim: redraw one segment slightly longer while retaining all stated incidence facts. The original assumptions remain true but equality fails.
practice.diagram: Two disjoint, unmarked segments of visibly similar lengths; a separate exact ruler panel [0, 5] and [7, 12]. Do not add equality marks in the initial panel.

practice.prompt: For n = 0, 1, 2 the values are 1, 3, 5. Does this show that f(n) = 2n + 1 works for every whole number n? Compare two rules at n = 6.
practice.slot: No drawing needed; live text only.
practice.solution: No. Both f(n)=2n+1 and g(n)=2n+1+n(n-1)(n-2) fit all three data points, but f(6)=13 and g(6)=133. A proof needs a rule or hypothesis controlling every n.
practice.check: Direct substitution n=0, 1, 2 makes the extra product zero each time; at n=6 all its factors are positive. This is an exact counterexample to uniqueness.
practice.diagram: No geometric diagram is needed; use live mathematical text.

practice.prompt: What do two different points determine? How are a line, a ray and a segment different?
practice.slot: Points A, B, C in a row, with blank panels for segment AB, ray AB and line AB.
practice.solution: Two distinct points determine exactly one line. Segment AB includes its two endpoints and points between them. Ray AB starts at A and extends through B without a second endpoint. The line extends both ways and has infinitely many points.
practice.check: A third collinear point lies on the same unique line; two coincident named points do not satisfy the distinctness hypothesis.
practice.diagram: A=(0, 0), B=(6, 0), C=(8, 0). Three panels: segment AB with endpoint dots, ray AB with one arrow, line AB with two arrows. No finite endpoint dot on a line.

practice.prompt: Model: the Earth is a sphere and sunlight is parallel. Two cities on one north-south circle are 600 km apart along the surface, with a center angle of 6 degrees. Estimate the distance around the Earth.
practice.slot: Circle O, cities A and B, a 6 degree angle at O, and the curved arc labeled 600 km.
practice.solution: The arc is 6/360 of a full circle, so C=600·360/6=36000 km. The shadow-angle to central-angle identification is a preview assumption here; its parallel-line proof comes in Unit 5.
practice.check: The circumference divided by 360 is 100 km per degree; 6 degrees then gives 600 km, matching the input.
practice.diagram: Circle O, cities A, B on same meridian section, central angle 6; parallel sunlight rays and local radius directions. City separation is curved arc 600, not chord.

practice.prompt: A convex polygon has 4 sides. How many vertices and sides does it have, and how many diagonals start at one vertex?
practice.slot: Convex four-sided polygon A1 to A4, with dashed diagonals from A1 only.
practice.solution: There are 4 vertices and 4 sides. From one vertex there are 3 other vertices; exclude its two neighbors, leaving 1 diagonal. This is counting, not an early assertion of the angle-sum formula.
practice.check: Total diagonal count would be 4(4-3)/2=2, since each diagonal is counted at both ends.
practice.diagram: Convex 4-gon A1, ..., A4 in circular order, diagonals from A1 only; no crossings in polygon boundary.

practice.prompt: Using only a compass and straightedge, copy a length of 5 onto a ray that starts at P. Explain why the copy is 5 long.
practice.slot: Segment AB = 5, and a ray from P with room for an arc.
practice.solution: Set the compass opening to the given segment. With center P draw an arc crossing the specified ray at Q. Since Q is on that radius-5 circle, PQ=5. The chosen ray fixes the intended forward intersection.
practice.check: Circle definition alone supplies the equality; neither a ruler reading nor triangle congruence is needed.
practice.diagram: Source segment AB=5; elsewhere ray PX and radius-5 arc centered P, forward intersection Q. Live labels AB, P, Q and retained construction arc.

practice.prompt: In our system, 'incidence' (a point lying on a line) is undefined. What does that mean? Can we assume anything we like about it?
practice.slot: No drawing needed; live text only.
practice.solution: It means we do not define 'lies on' with other words. We start with it and write rules about it. Undefined does not mean anything goes: the rules limit what can happen. Theorems are then proved from those rules and our definitions.
practice.check: Interpret the same incidence axioms in two different labeled diagrams. Renaming points does not change truth; adding an unlicensed incidence can violate an axiom. This separates vocabulary from constraints.
practice.diagram: No geometric diagram is needed; use live mathematical text.

practice.prompt: n is an integer. Write the contrapositive of 'if n is divisible by 10, then n is divisible by 5.' Then prove the original statement from the definitions.
practice.slot: Two nested circles: 'divisible by 10' inside 'divisible by 5'.
practice.solution: If n=10k for an integer k, then n=5(2k), so n is divisible by 5. Contrapositive: if n is not divisible by 5, then n is not divisible by 10.
practice.check: The inclusion of integer multiples of 10 among multiples of 5 checks the original; the logical truth table checks equivalence with the contrapositive.
practice.diagram: Divisibility-class inclusion diagram with the declared integer domain.

practice.prompt: Is 'a quadrilateral with at least one right angle' a good definition of a rectangle? If not, write a correct one.
practice.slot: No drawing needed; live text only.
practice.solution: The proposed condition admits a quadrilateral with given angles of 90, 60, 120 and 90 degrees, so it is not sufficient. Exact replacement: rectangle if and only if quadrilateral with four right angles. Both necessity and sufficiency are part of the definition.
practice.check: Check the replacement in each direction: a named rectangle satisfies the condition by the adopted definition; any object satisfying the full condition is a rectangle. The original counterexample no longer qualifies.
practice.diagram: No geometric diagram is needed; use live mathematical text.

practice.prompt: Prove that the sum of two multiples of 3 is a multiple of 3.
practice.slot: No drawing needed; live text only.
practice.solution: By the definition of a multiple, m=3r and n=3s for integers r, s. Then m+n=3r+3s=3(r+s). Since integers are closed under addition, r+s is an integer, so m+n is a multiple of 3.
practice.check: Difference is a parallel independent result: m-n=3(r-s). The sum proof uses only a definition, distributivity and integer closure, not selected numerical cases.
practice.diagram: No geometric diagram is needed; use live mathematical text.

practice.prompt: Prove indirectly: if an integer's square is odd, the integer is odd. Use it when the square is 49, and check n = 7.
practice.slot: No drawing needed; live text only.
practice.solution: Assume n² is odd but n is not odd. Every integer is even or odd, so n=2k for an integer k. Then n²=4k²=2(2k²) is even, contradicting the given odd square. Therefore n is odd. For the specified square the possible integers are plus or minus 7, both odd. n²=49 is odd and n=7 is odd; this check illustrates the proved universal statement, not a replacement for its proof.
practice.check: The contrapositive supplies a second route: an even integer 2k has even square 4k². This is equivalent to the claim. No ruler postulate, triangle theorem or drawing is used.
practice.diagram: No geometric diagram is needed; use live mathematical text.

practice.prompt: A made-up rule says z = 2x + 1, and you are given x = 4. Which part is the definition, which is the given, and which is the result?
practice.slot: Three boxes: input, rule, output (output left blank).
practice.solution: The rule z=2x+1 is the given definition of the operation. x=4 is the given input. Substitution derives z=2·4+1=9; the output 9 is a result, not another assumption.
practice.check: Running the inverse calculation (9 - 1)/2 returns 4. All required rules are printed here; no ruler or midpoint theorem is used.

practice.prompt: The same segment PQ has two written labels in the same units: PQ = 4 and PQ = 6. The drawing says 'not to scale.' Does that note fix the conflict? Could redrawing the segment make both labels true?
practice.slot: One segment PQ with two GIVEN boxes, PQ = 4 and PQ = 6, and a NOT TO SCALE caption. Only one segment is drawn.
practice.solution: No to both. One length cannot equal two different numbers in the same units. Not to scale permits a schematic picture, not contradictory exact data. One written datum must be corrected or the problem must be declared inconsistent; changing the pixels cannot satisfy both.
practice.check: Substituting PQ=4 into PQ=6 would give 4=6, which is false independently of every drawing. Changing display scale does not change either asserted numerical value.
practice.diagram: One segment PQ with two separate GIVEN boxes, PQ=4 and PQ=6, and a NOT TO SCALE caption. Reveal the conflicting equation 4=6 in a text panel. Do not draw two different segments or silently choose one label.

practice.prompt: A designer checks some triangles and other closed paths that don't cross themselves, then guesses: every closed path made of straight segments is a simple polygon. A new card shows the closed path A-B-C-D-A and says that sides AB and CD cross at X, inside both sides. What does this card show? Could more examples that work save the guess?
practice.slot: Two cards with simple closed paths, then a bow-tie card with the printed given 'X is inside both AB and CD'. No coordinates on the student card.
practice.solution: The card refutes the universal conjecture. Its path is closed and straight-edged, so it meets the hypothesis, but the stated nonconsecutive crossing violates the definition of a simple polygon. More successful examples cannot erase this valid counterexample. A narrower replacement conjecture would require its own justification.
practice.check: Write H for closed and straight-edged, and S for simple polygon. The card has H true and S false, exactly the false case for H implies S. The conclusion uses the given crossing, not an apparent crossing inferred from pixels.
practice.diagram: Show two checked simple-path cards and a third bow-tie card with A=(0,0), B=(4,4), C=(0,4), D=(4,0), X=(2,2). Explicitly print X IS INTERIOR TO BOTH AB AND CD as given information. Coordinates are builder-only; no midpoint computation is assigned.

A.prompt: On a construction sheet, two angles carry the same arc mark, but one is drawn much wider than the other. The sheet says matching arc marks are givens. What can you conclude? What should be fixed in the drawing?
A.slot: Two angles named alpha and beta, each with one arc mark. One is drawn too wide and labeled 'not to scale'.
A.solution: The angles are congruent because the given marks are givens. The inaccurate rendering should be corrected; the drawing does not cancel an explicit hypothesis. No numerical angle measure follows without a degree label.
A.check: Erase the picture and retain the written equal-mark convention: congruence still follows, while a numerical value remains undetermined.
A.diagram: Two angle panels labeled alpha, beta with identical single arcs; one deliberately distorted panel is flagged not to scale.

A.prompt: Someone claims f(n) = n² + n + 41 gives a prime for every whole number n. (A prime is a whole number greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself.) Work out f(40) exactly. Is the claim true?
A.slot: Flow boxes: 40, then the formula, then an empty output box.
A.solution: f(40)=1600+40+41=1681=41². Thus 41 is a positive divisor other than 1 or 1681, so the value is not prime. The single input 40 refutes the universal conjecture, regardless of how many smaller cases worked.
A.check: Factor directly: 40²+40+41=40·41+41=41(40+1)=41². This factorization independently checks the decimal arithmetic.
A.diagram: Input 40 flows through the displayed formula to 1681; the output is factored into 41×41. No geometric diagram is needed.

A.prompt: Lines l and m are different and cross at P. Q is on l but is not P. R is on m but is not P. Can the line through Q and R also go through P? Use only facts about which points lie on which lines.
A.slot: Points P, Q, R with line l through P and Q, line m through P and R, and the line through Q and R. Every line has arrows.
A.solution: No. If QR passed through P, uniqueness for P, Q would make it l. It would then contain P, R, so uniqueness for P, R would make it m. This forces l=m, a contradiction.
A.check: In the valid configuration, the three connecting lines PQ, PR, QR form a triangle of incidences, not three lines through P. No angle or length theorem is used.
A.diagram: P=(0, 0), Q=(4, 0), R=(1, 3); l=PQ, m=PR, third line QR; all full lines have arrows.

A.prompt: A made-up round planet has a circumference of 43,200 km. Two sites on one north-south circle are 900 km apart along the surface. If every degree of center angle matches the same arc length, what is the center angle? Name one assumption you would need to say this equals a shadow angle.
A.slot: Circle O with an arc labeled 900 km, the circumference labeled 43,200 km and the center angle marked '?'. A separate sunlight sketch is labeled 'assumed'.
A.solution: Angle=360·900/43,200=7.5 degrees. Identifying it with a shadow angle additionally requires the specified meridian arrangement and parallel sunlight, together with the later parallel-angle justification. That identification is a preview assumption, not proved here.
A.diagram: Circle O with meridian arc 900 km, total circumference 43,200 km, central angle unknown; separate parallel-sunlight schematic labeled assumed.

A.prompt: A pen moves from A = (0, 0) to B = (4, 0) to C = (4, 3) to D = (0, 3) and stops. Is this path a polygon yet? Which single straight segment would finish a simple four-sided polygon?
A.slot: The open three-sided path on a grid. The finishing segment is left for the student to draw.
A.solution: The trace is open, so it is not a polygon boundary. Add DA. This joins the remaining endpoint D to A without crossing the other edges and closes the four-sided chain.
A.check: Before you add DA, A and D each touch only one drawn side. After you add DA, every corner touches exactly two sides, so the path is closed.
A.diagram: Exact three-sided open rectangular trace; dashed proposed closing segment DA, then a separate closed-chain reveal.

A.prompt: A circle centered at M and a circle centered at N have the same radius r. They share the point X. The distance MN is not given. Which of MX, NX and MN must equal r? Use only definitions.
A.slot: Two overlapping circles with equal-radius marks, centers M and N, and shared point X. No coordinates shown.
A.solution: MX=NX=r because X lies on both circles. MN need not equal r: equal radii do not specify the distance between centers. No congruence theorem is needed.
A.check: Choose centers distance r apart for one model and 1.5r apart for another; both allow overlapping equal-radius circles, but the center distances differ. Only the stated circle incidences force the radius equalities.
A.diagram: Two overlapping circles of radius 2, centers M=(-1.5, 0), N=(1.5, 0), upper crossing X=(0, sqrt(7)/2). Coordinates are builder-only; student data are equal radii and common-point marks.

A.prompt: A made-up system has four points and only two lines: {A, B} and {C, D}. Its one rule is 'every point is on exactly one line.' Does the system follow the rule? Does the rule force all the points onto one line?
A.slot: A table with four point rows and two line columns. No arrowheads.
A.solution: Yes, the listed model satisfies the axiom because each point appears in exactly one listed line. No, it does not force one common line; this very model is a counterexample. This is a toy system, not a claim that its finite lines satisfy Euclidean axioms.
A.check: Count line memberships: A, B, C, D each have 1. Neither of the two line sets contains all four points.
A.diagram: Incidence table with four point rows and two line columns; do not draw arrowheads suggesting complete Euclidean lines.

A.prompt: A bin holds two compasses, C1 and C2, and one straightedge, S. All three are metal. For this bin, decide whether each claim is true: 'every compass is metal' and 'every metal object is a compass.' For a false claim, name an object that shows it.
A.slot: Three inventory cards with columns COMPASS and METAL.
A.solution: The first is true on this stated finite bin: C1, C2 are metal. The second is false because S is metal but is a straightedge, not a compass. The claims are converse implications, not equivalent definitions.
A.check: Exhaust the 3 listed objects. S has Metal=true, Compass=false, the exact truth pattern falsifying 'if Metal then Compass'.
A.diagram: Three labeled inventory cards with columns COMPASS and METAL; no color coding.

A.prompt: A 'triad' means three different points that are not all on one line. A proposed test is 'the record lists three point names.' Give two different records that pass the test but are not triads. Then write an exact 'if and only if' test.
A.slot: Three empty panels for the student's records.
A.solution: A record A, A, B has repeated points; A, B, C with three collinear locations has distinct names but still fails. A record is a triad if and only if it names exactly three different points and no one line holds all three.
A.check: A noncollinear triangle passes the repaired test. Each false positive fails a different required condition, so both conditions are needed.
A.diagram: Three panels: repeated-name record; three dots on one line; three noncollinear dots.

A.prompt: You are given a = b + c and b = d + e. Prove a = d + e + c. A classmate writes c = d + e instead. Which statement follows, and why?
A.slot: No drawing needed; live text only.
A.solution: Substitute b=d+e into a=b+c: a=(d+e)+c=d+e+c. Nothing identifies c with b, so c=d+e does not follow.
A.check: Counterexample to the extra assertion: d=1, e=2, c=4, b=3, a=7 satisfies both givens, but c is 4, not 3. The proved equation gives 7=1+2+4.
A.diagram: Dependency tree with b feeding into the expression for a; the unsupported c=b edge is crossed out.

A.prompt: Use only these two rules: x < x is never true, and if x < y and y < z, then x < z. Prove that a < b and b < a can't both be true.
A.slot: Two arrows, a to b and b to a.
A.solution: Assume both. The second rule turns a < b and b < a into a < a. The first rule says a < a is never true. That is a contradiction, so the two can't both be true.
A.check: The same substitution with roles reversed also gives b<b. Either violates the first printed rule.
A.diagram: Two directed strict-order arrows a→b and b→a, with the derived forbidden self-loop shown in the reveal.

A.prompt: A system has three assumptions. S: every marked point is on line l. T: point P is marked. U: P is not on l. Can all three be true together? Show that removing any one of them gets rid of this contradiction.
A.slot: A blank table with columns 'P marked' and 'P on l'.
A.solution: Together S and T put P on l, contradicting U. Delete U: put marked P on l. Delete T: put unmarked P off l and use no marked points. Delete S: put marked P off l. Thus all three assumptions together are inconsistent, and every two-assumption subset has a model.
A.check: Write M for 'P is marked' and L for 'P is on l.' The assumptions are 'if M then L', 'M', and 'not L'. Try all four true/false rows for M and L: no row makes all three true, but every pair of them is true in some row.
A.diagram: A three-rule dependency diagram and a four-row Boolean table M, L. Tiny witness panels label marked/unmarked by text, not color.

B.prompt: A circle has two chords that look equal, with no marks. Eli writes 'the chords are congruent because the picture is symmetric.' What information, if it were given, would make that a fair given? What is still unproved in the drawing as it is?
B.slot: Circle with chords AB and CD and no tick marks.
B.solution: An explicit chord-equality mark or a written equality could supply that equality as a given. As drawn, neither congruence nor an exact symmetry was specified or proved. Merely looking symmetric is insufficient.
B.check: Move one chord’s endpoint along the same circle while preserving the stated circle incidence; the chord lengths can differ. This retains every actual hypothesis.
B.diagram: Circle with chords AB, CD and no equality ticks; second admissible panel shifts D. No radius/chord theorem is invoked.

B.prompt: A sequence starts at u0 = 2, and each term is the one before plus 3: u(n + 1) = u(n) + 3 for every whole number n. Find u3. Why is this deduction and not a guess from a pattern?
B.slot: A chain of four boxes, with '+ 3' on each arrow and the rule printed above.
B.solution: The rule gives u1=5, u2=8, u3=11. Each step follows an explicitly supplied rule, so it is deductive. A bare list 2, 5, 8 without the rule would not establish a unique continuation.
B.check: Reverse each step by subtracting 3: 11→8→5→2. The given universal recurrence, not a visual pattern, licenses those steps.
B.diagram: Four-node recurrence chain with+3 on each arrow and the universal rule printed above.

B.prompt: Four survey markers are all different, and no three of them are on one line. A report says only five lines are needed to connect every pair of markers. Show the report is wrong without measuring any angles.
B.slot: Four markers A, B, C, D, no three in a line, with room to draw the lines.
B.solution: There are 6 unordered pairs. If two different pairs determined the same full line, their union would contain at least 3 distinct collinear markers, contradicting the hypothesis. Thus all 6 lines are distinct; five is impossible.
B.check: List AB, AC, AD, BC, BD, CD. The no-three-collinear condition prevents every possible collapse of two pair-lines.
B.diagram: A=(0, 0), B=(4, 0), C=(1, 3), D=(5, 4); six pair-lines with arrows. These coordinates have no collinear triple.

B.prompt: On one round-planet model, a 9 degree north-south arc is 1,000 km long. On another it is 1,500 km. Using the same 'equal arc for each degree' rule, which planet is bigger around, and what is the ratio?
B.slot: Two circles, each with a 9 degree center angle, arcs labeled 1,000 km and 1,500 km.
B.solution: Both arcs are 9/360=1/40 of a full circle. Circumferences are 40,000 and 60,000 km, so the second is larger with ratio 3: 2. This is arithmetic within the given spherical models, not an unproved general similarity theorem.
B.check: 60,000/40,000=1,500/1,000=3/2. Multiplying each circumference by 1/40 returns its own given arc.
B.diagram: Two circle schematics with identical 9 degree central angles and separately labeled 1,000 and 1,500 km arcs; not a chord comparison.

B.prompt: A simple five-sided region has B and D on its boundary. Point W lies between B and D but outside the region; these facts are given. Is the region convex? Which part of the definition fails?
B.slot: A five-sided shape with a dent, a dashed segment from B to D, and W marked on it outside the shape. Only B, D and W are labeled.
B.solution: It is not convex. Both endpoints B, D belong to the region, but their joining segment contains W outside it. This directly violates the requirement that every such joining segment stay in the region.
B.check: The statement “every joining segment stays inside” is refuted by the single witness segment BD and its point W. No distance, slope or triangle-angle theorem is needed.
B.diagram: Builder certificate only: A=(0, 0), B=(4, 0), C=(2, 1), D=(4, 4), E=(0, 4), W=(4, 2). Show the concave boundary and dashed BD. Student labels are only B, D, W and the stipulated outside incidence.

B.prompt: Circle c has center P and passes through Q, where P and Q are different. Circle d has center Q and passes through P. The two radii are equal. Are c and d the same circle? Decide by checking whether P is on each one.
B.slot: Points P and Q, with a circle around each passing through the other center.
B.solution: No. P belongs to d because d was drawn through P. P does not belong to c: its distance from c’s center P is 0, less than the positive radius PQ. Thus one set contains a point the other does not.
B.check: Q supplies the opposite witness: Q is in c but not in d. Equal radius does not imply identical centers or identical circles.
B.diagram: P=(0, 0), Q=(3, 0), two radius 3 circles centered at the respective points; label membership witnesses without requiring any circle-congruence theorem.

B.prompt: A system's only assumptions are 'A implies B' and 'B implies C.' Show that A implies C. Must 'C implies A' also follow? Give true or false values for A, B and C to back up your answer.
B.slot: Arrow chain A to B to C, with an empty truth-value table below.
B.solution: If A is true, the first rule gives B and the second gives C, so 'if A then C' holds. The reverse need not hold: with A false, B false and C true, both rules are true, but 'if C then A' is false.
B.check: An if-then is false only when its 'if' part is true and its 'then' part is false.
B.diagram: Three-node implication chain A→B→C, with the counterassignment printed in a separate table.

B.prompt: A device rule says 'if the switch is on, then the lamp is on.' Four observations of (switch, lamp) are (off, off), (off, on), (on, on) and (on, off). Which one breaks the rule? Does seeing the lamp on prove the switch is on?
B.slot: Four observation cards labeled SWITCH and LAMP, with ON or OFF written in words.
B.solution: Only (on, off) violates the implication. An on lamp does not certify an on switch because (off, on) is explicitly observed and does not violate the contract.
B.check: Map switch/lamp to (P, Q). The violating row is (T, F); the reverse inference is refuted by (F, T).
B.diagram: Four observation cards labeled SWITCH, LAMP and ON/OFF in text; no colored status lights.

B.prompt: A database calls a pair of real numbers (x, y) 'reciprocal.' Its test is x + y = 1. Find a pair that passes the test but shouldn't, a pair that fails but should pass, and the correct exact test.
B.slot: A table with columns PAIR, SUM and PRODUCT.
B.solution: False positive: (2, -1) has sum 1 but product -2. False negative: (2, 1/2) has product 1 but sum 2.5. Correct test: xy=1, which also forces both entries nonzero.
B.check: Compute the two products and sums independently. If xy=1, then y=1/x and x=1/y; conversely either reciprocal relation gives product 1.
B.diagram: Two pair records with SUM and PRODUCT columns; an exact “xy=1” validator below.

B.prompt: Solve x² = x for real numbers. A classmate divides both sides by x right away and gets only x = 1. Find every solution and the case that was lost.
B.slot: No drawing needed; live text only.
B.solution: Move terms: x²-x=x(x-1)=0. The zero-product rule gives x=0 or x=1. Dividing by x only works if x is not 0, so it throws away the solution x = 0.
B.check: Substitution gives 0²=0 and 1²=1. For x not 0 or 1, neither factor is zero, so there is no additional solution.
B.diagram: Algebra branch diagram x=0 and x-1=0; the division step is labeled conditional onx≠0.

B.prompt: You are given two rules: 'H implies E' and 'H implies not E.' Prove 'not H' by contradiction. Don't assume E or not E before you start.
B.slot: A fork: H leads to E on one branch and to not E on the other.
B.solution: Assume H. The first rule derives E, and the second derives not E. The contradiction E and not E rejects H, so not H. Both branches are necessary to expose the contradiction.
B.check: In a truth table, any row with H=true makes at least one of the two given implications false. All rows satisfying both have H=false.
B.diagram: H branches to E and not E; the fork joins at a contradiction marker, then not H is the conclusion.

B.prompt: System U assumes exactly one line through every two distinct points. System E assumes at least one line through every two distinct points and does not assume uniqueness. (In plain words: For every pair of different points, U requires exactly one line through both points. E requires at least one line through both points, but allows either one or more than one.) Does 'two different lines can't share two different points' hold in both systems? If not, build a small example that breaks it.
B.slot: A blank table with point rows and line columns.
B.solution: It follows in U by uniqueness. It need not follow in E: take points P, Q, R, S and line-sets l={P, Q, R}, m={P, Q, S}, n={R, S}. Every point pair has at least one listed line, but distinct l, m both contain P, Q. This is a toy incidence example that fits E, not a Euclidean plane.
B.check: List six pairs: PQ lies on l, m; PR, QR on l; PS, QS on m; RS on n. Every pair of points has at least one line, so system E's rule holds. But P and Q are on two different lines, l and m, so 'exactly one line' fails.
B.diagram: Four-point/three-line incidence table for the given sets; highlight the two PQ memberships.
